claim: Quiescent stem cells are activated in response to a mechanical or chemical injury to their tissue niche.
source: Quiescent stem cells are activated in response to a mechanical or chemical injury to their tissue niche.
evidence: This is a general statement about stem cell biology presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Activated cells rapidly generate a heterogeneous progenitor population that regenerates the damaged tissues.
source: Activated cells rapidly generate a heterogeneous progenitor population that regenerates the damaged tissues.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in stem cell biology and is consistent with the experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mitochondrial glutamine metabolism induces CBP/EP300-dependent acetylation of PASK.
source: We discovered that mitochondrial glutamine metabolism induces CBP/EP300-dependent acetylation of stem cell-specific kinase, PAS domain-containing kinase (PASK), resulting in its release from cytoplasmic granules and subsequent nuclear migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that glutamine metabolism drives PASK acetylation via CBP/EP300 (Figure 4C, 4F-H).

claim: CBP/EP300-dependent acetylation of PASK results in its release from cytoplasmic granules and subsequent nuclear migration.
source: We discovered that mitochondrial glutamine metabolism induces CBP/EP300-dependent acetylation of stem cell-specific kinase, PAS domain-containing kinase (PASK), resulting in its release from cytoplasmic granules and subsequent nuclear migration.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that CBP/EP300 inhibition blocks PASK nuclear translocation (Figure 4D, 4I) and that PASK is localized in cytoplasmic granules in proliferating cells (Figure 2A, 2C).

claim: Nuclear PASK catalytically outcompetes mitotic WDR5-APC/C interaction resulting in the loss of post-mitotic Pax7 expression and exit from self-renewal.
source: In the nucleus, PASK catalytically outcompetes mitotic WDR5-anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) interaction resulting in the loss of post-mitotic Pax7 expression and exit from self-renewal.
evidence: This is supported by data showing PASK disrupts WDR5-APC/C interaction (Figure 7C-F) and that PASK activity is required for downregulation of Pax7 (Figure 6A-B, 7G-J).

claim: Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PASK upregulated Pax7 expression.
source: In concordance with these findings, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PASK or glutamine metabolism upregulated Pax7 expression, reduced stem cell heterogeneity, and blocked myogenesis in vitro and muscle regeneration in mice.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased Pax7+ cells in PASKi-treated (Figure 6A-B) and PaskKO myoblasts (Figure 1E-F).

claim: Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of glutamine metabolism upregulated Pax7 expression.
source: In concordance with these findings, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PASK or glutamine metabolism upregulated Pax7 expression, reduced stem cell heterogeneity, and blocked myogenesis in vitro and muscle regeneration in mice.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased Pax7+ cells upon glutamine withdrawal (Figure 5B-E) and BPTES treatment (Figure 5J-K).

claim: Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PASK reduced stem cell heterogeneity.
source: In concordance with these findings, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PASK or glutamine metabolism upregulated Pax7 expression, reduced stem cell heterogeneity, and blocked myogenesis in vitro and muscle regeneration in mice.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced heterogeneity in Pax7 expression levels in PASKi-treated cells (Figure 6A-B) and PaskKO cells (Figure 1E-F).

claim: Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PASK blocked myogenesis in vitro.
source: In concordance with these findings, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PASK or glutamine metabolism upregulated Pax7 expression, reduced stem cell heterogeneity, and blocked myogenesis in vitro and muscle regeneration in mice.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced MyoG+ cells and fusion index in PaskKO myoblasts (Figure 1E-G) and blocked differentiation with PASKi treatment (Figure 1C).

claim: Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PASK blocked muscle regeneration in mice.
source: In concordance with these findings, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PASK or glutamine metabolism upregulated Pax7 expression, reduced stem cell heterogeneity, and blocked myogenesis in vitro and muscle regeneration in mice.
evidence: This is supported by data showing decreased eMHC+ myofibers in PaskKO mice (Figure 1H-J) and smaller myofiber cross-sectional areas at 14 dpi (Figure 6E).

claim: Self-renewing stem cells rapidly reactivate the expression of genes linked with cell identity following cell division.
source: To preserve stem cell identity, self-renewing stem cells rapidly reactivate the expression of genes linked with cell identity following cell division.
evidence: This is established knowledge in stem cell biology cited in the introduction.

claim: Mitotic recruitment of APC/C by WDR5 to transcriptional start sites regulates post-mitotic reactivation of lineage-defining genes.
source: Several mechanisms have been proposed for the post-mitotic reactivation of lineage-defining genes, including the mitotic recruitment of the E3 ubiquitin ligase anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) by WDR5 to transcriptional start sites of genes regulating pluripotency and H3K27ac mitotic bookmarking (Pelham-Webb et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2017; Oh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Pelham-Webb et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2017; Oh et al., 2020).

claim: H3K27ac mitotic bookmarking regulates post-mitotic reactivation of lineage-defining genes.
source: Several mechanisms have been proposed for the post-mitotic reactivation of lineage-defining genes, including the mitotic recruitment of the E3 ubiquitin ligase anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) by WDR5 to transcriptional start sites of genes regulating pluripotency and H3K27ac mitotic bookmarking (Pelham-Webb et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2017; Oh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Pelham-Webb et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2017; Oh et al., 2020).

claim: The WDR5-APC/C interaction is enhanced during mitosis.
source: During mitosis, the WDR5-APC/C interaction is enhanced, and transient disruption of this interaction causes loss of pluripotency in embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Oh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Oh et al., 2020).

claim: Transient disruption of the WDR5-APC/C interaction causes loss of pluripotency in embryonic stem cells.
source: During mitosis, the WDR5-APC/C interaction is enhanced, and transient disruption of this interaction causes loss of pluripotency in embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Oh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Oh et al., 2020).

claim: Expression of PASK positively correlates with the undifferentiated, proliferative state of ESCs and adult stem cells.
source: Expression of PAS domain-containing kinase (PASK), a kinase involved in cellular energy balance and metabolic control, positively correlates with the undifferentiated, proliferative state of ESCs and adult stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2019; Kikani et al., 2016).

claim: PASK is required for the onset of ESC and adult stem cell differentiation programs downstream of nutrient signaling.
source: Functionally, PASK is required for the onset of ESC and adult stem cell differentiation programs downstream of nutrient signaling (Kikani et al., 2019; Kikani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kikani et al., 2019; Kikani et al., 2016).

claim: PASK is required to induce an early regenerative myogenesis program in adult muscles.
source: In adult muscles, PASK is required to induce an early regenerative myogenesis program (Kikani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2016).

claim: PASK is required to generate the MyoD+, MyoG+ committed progenitor population during myogenesis.
source: We and others have shown that PASK is required to generate the MyoD+, MyoG+ committed progenitor population during myogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by data in the manuscript (Figure 1E-G) and citations to prior work.

claim: PASK phosphorylates WDR5 in response to differentiation signaling.
source: Mechanistically, PASK phosphorylates WDR5, a member of the histone H3 lysine 4 methyltransferase (H3K4me3) complexes, in response to differentiation signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kikani et al., 2019; Kikani et al., 2016; Karakkat et al., 2019).

claim: Phosphorylation of WDR5 by PASK sets in motion chromatin remodeling at the Myog promoter and its transcriptional activation.
source: This phosphorylation sets in motion chromatin remodeling at the Myog promoter and its transcriptional activation resulting in the onset of myogenesis (Kikani et al., 2019; Kikani et al., 2016; Karakkat et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kikani et al., 2019; Kikani et al., 2016; Karakkat et al., 2019).

claim: mTOR-dependent phosphorylation of PASK stimulates the PASK-WDR5 interaction.
source: This entire pathway is downstream of nutrient-activated mTOR-dependent phosphorylation of PASK, which stimulates the PASK-WDR5 interaction (Kikani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2019).

claim: PASK function is specifically required to establish the initial committed myoblast progenitor population but is dispensable to sustain myogenesis.
source: Intriguingly, the PASK function is specifically required to establish the initial committed myoblast progenitor population but is dispensable to sustain myogenesis (Kikani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2019).

claim: Signaling cues from the early regenerating niche play critical regulatory roles in facilitating the transition from quiescent, non-proliferative MuSCs to activated, hyper-proliferative myoblasts.
source: Signaling cues from the early regenerating niche play critical regulatory roles in facilitating the transition from quiescent, non-proliferative MuSCs to activated, hyper-proliferative myoblasts during the early stages of tissue regeneration (Ryall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Ryall et al., 2015).

claim: Mitochondrial uptake of glutamine plays an essential role in sustaining stem cell proliferation by generating ATP and maintaining redox balance.
source: Mitochondrial uptake of glutamine is thought to play an essential role in sustaining stem cell proliferation by generating ATP and maintaining redox balance (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Yu et al., 2019).

claim: Glutamine secreted by macrophages sustains myoblast proliferation and promotes differentiation during muscle regeneration.
source: During muscle regeneration, glutamine secreted by macrophages sustains myoblast proliferation and promotes differentiation (Shang et al., 2020); however, the precise mechanistic function of glutamine metabolism in driving myoblast differentiation is unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Shang et al., 2020).

claim: Glutamine metabolic signaling is required to generate a differentiation-primed progenitor population by disrupting the cell cycle-linked WDR5-APC/C interaction via PASK acetylation and nuclear localization.
source: In this pathway, glutamine metabolic signaling is required to generate a differentiation-primed progenitor population by disrupting the cell cycle-linked WDR5-APC/C interaction via PASK acetylation and nuclear localization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing glutamine drives PASK acetylation and nuclear translocation (Figure 4G-I), and that PASK disrupts WDR5-APC/C interaction (Figure 7C-F).

claim: Replacing 2i media with PASKi in mESCs resulted in a further increase in the expression of genes associated with self-renewal and stemness (Pou5f1, Sox2, and Prex1 mRNA) when compared with mESCs cultured in the 2i conditions.
source: Strikingly, replacing 2i media with PASKi in mESCs resulted in a further increase in the expression of genes associated with self-renewal and stemness (Pou5f1, Sox2, and Prex1 mRNA) when compared with mESCs cultured in the 2i conditions (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cells cultured in PASKi maintained Rex1-GFP reporter expression at levels comparable to those cultured in 2i.
source: Additionally, using a Rex1-GFP reporter mESC line (Wray et al., 2011), we observed that cells cultured in PASKi maintained GFP reporter expression at levels comparable to those cultured in 2i (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B and citation to the Rex1-GFP reporter line (Wray et al., 2011).

claim: PASKi cultured cells showed a substantial increase in the numbers and size of fluid-filled cavitated structures compared with 2i pretreated cells (~52% for PASKi versus ~12% for 2i-treated cells) after PASKi withdrawal.
source: Remarkably, PASKi cultured cells showed a substantial increase in the numbers and size of fluid-filled cavitated structures compared with 2i pretreated cells (~52% for PASKi versus ~12% for 2i-treated cells, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) after PASKi withdrawal.
evidence: This is supported by embryoid body formation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The presence of PASKi during EB formation attenuated differentiation as assessed morphologically.
source: Consistent with our previous study, the presence of PASKi during EB formation attenuated differentiation as assessed morphologically (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Kikani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by morphological data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2016).

claim: PASK inhibition preserves self-renewal and enhances differentiation potential upon PASK inhibitor withdrawal in ESCs.
source: Thus, PASK inhibition in ESCs preserved self-renewal and enhanced differentiation potential upon PASK inhibitor withdrawal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing increased stemness markers with PASKi (Figure 1A-B) and enhanced EB formation after PASKi withdrawal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: PASK is highly expressed in adult proliferating stem cells.
source: PASK is highly expressed in adult proliferating stem cells (Kikani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2016).

claim: PASK expression is negligible in adult quiescent MuSCs but increases rapidly as MuSCs are activated and begin to proliferate.
source: While PASK is expressed at negligible levels in adult quiescent MuSCs, its expression increases rapidly as MuSCs are activated and begin to proliferate (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Kikani et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and citations to prior work (Kikani et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2013).

claim: PASK inhibition robustly blocked the precocious myogenesis observed in the control myoblasts for as long as 4 days post-isolation.
source: On the other hand, PASKi robustly blocked the precocious myogenesis observed in the control myoblasts for as long as 4 days post-isolation (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and MHC staining data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: PASK inhibition preserves the self-renewal property of cultured ESCs and adult MuSCs and prevents their precocious differentiation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that PASK inhibition preserves the self-renewal property of cultured ESCs and adult MuSCs and prevents their precocious differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations in ESCs and MuSCs showing increased stemness markers and blocked differentiation with PASKi.

claim: MuSCs isolated from PaskWT or PaskKO were indistinguishable in size 12 hr post-isolation and did not show overt proliferation defects.
source: MuSCs isolated from PaskWT or PaskKO were indistinguishable in size 12 hr post-isolation and did not show overt proliferation defects, which is consistent with our previous results and the notion that PASK is not expressed or required for the maintenance or release from a quiescent state.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and inference from prior work.

claim: PaskWT cells began to form nascent myotubes by 48 hr post-isolation, while PaskKO cells continued to proliferate and showed little signs of myotube formation.
source: Finally, while PaskWT cells began to form nascent myotubes by 48 hr post-isolation, PaskKO cells continued to proliferate and showed little signs of myotube formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Genetic or pharmacological loss of PASK results in continued self-renewal of adult myoblasts and impaired differentiation.
source: Thus, genetic or pharmacological loss of PASK results in continued self-renewal of adult myoblasts and impaired differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing increased Pax7+ cells and reduced differentiation in PaskKO and PASKi-treated myoblasts.

claim: Quiescent MuSCs express Pax7 but lack MyoD or Myf5 protein expression.
source: Quiescent MuSCs express Pax7 but lack MyoD or Myf5 protein expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing gene expression patterns.

claim: Upon isolation, Pax7+ MuSCs rapidly activate MyoD mRNA translation, and by 48 hr, Pax7+/MyoD+ SCs diverge into a heterogeneous population expressing a combination of Pax7, MyoD, and/or Myf5.
source: Upon their isolation, Pax7+ MuSCs rapidly activate MyoD mRNA translation, and by 48 hr, Pax7+/MyoD+ SCs diverge into a heterogeneous population expressing a combination of Pax7, MyoD, and/or Myf5 (Figure 1D–E; Rocheteau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1D-E and citation to prior literature (Rocheteau et al., 2012).

claim: PaskKO MuSCs showed an increased percentage of Pax7+ myoblasts numbers compared with control (~83% for PaskKO vs. 30% for PaskWT) during 48 hr of culture.
source: Interestingly, PaskKO MuSCs showed an increased percentage of Pax7+ myoblasts numbers compared with control (~83% for PaskKO vs. 30% for PaskWT) during 48 hr of culture.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Loss of PASK resulted in reduced levels of MyoD+ myoblasts.
source: Similarly, loss of PASK resulted in reduced levels of MyoD+ myoblasts (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 1E-F.

claim: The increased proportion of Pax7+ myoblasts observed in PaskKO is independent of the method chosen for stem cell isolation (FACS, MACS, and pronase-based method).
source: Furthermore, the increased proportion of Pax7+ myoblasts observed in PaskKO is independent of the method chosen for stem cell isolation (FACS, magnetic-activated cell sorting [MACS], and pronase-based method) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-D.

claim: PaskKO myoblasts showed a marked reduction in committed MyoG-expressing cells and myogenesis, as measured by the fusion index.
source: Finally, PaskKO myoblasts showed a marked reduction in committed MyoG-expressing cells and myogenesis, as measured by the fusion index (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and fusion index data in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Genetic loss of PASK increases self-renewing Pax7+ myoblast numbers and decreases the generation of committed (MyoD+/MyoG+) myoblasts in vitro.
source: Thus, genetic loss of PASK increases self-renewing Pax7+ myoblast numbers and decreases the generation of committed (MyoD+/MyoG+) myoblasts in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing increased Pax7+ and decreased MyoD+/MyoG+ cells in PaskKO myoblasts (Figure 1E-G).

claim: Loss of PASK severely affected the progression through the regenerative myogenesis program, as seen from decreased eMHC+ myofiber numbers in PaskKO animals compared with littermate controls 5 days post-injury.
source: Loss of PASK severely affected the progression through the regenerative myogenesis program, as seen from decreased eMHC+ myofiber numbers in PaskKO animals compared with littermate controls 5 days post-injury (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This is supported by eMHC staining and quantification data in Figure 1H-J.

claim: Loss of PASK resulted in a significant expansion of Pax7+ MuSC numbers in PaskKO muscles compared to the littermate control.
source: Furthermore, loss of PASK resulted in a significant expansion of Pax7+ MuSC numbers in PaskKO muscles compared to the littermate control (Figure 1K–L).
evidence: This is supported by Pax7 immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 1K-L.

claim: The loss of PASK impairs the transition from Pax7+ stem cells to the MyoD+/MyoG+ committed progenitor population required for the onset of the differentiation program.
source: Thus, the loss of PASK impairs the transition from Pax7+ stem cells to the MyoD+/MyoG+ committed progenitor population required for the onset of the differentiation program.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing increased Pax7+ cells, decreased MyoD+/MyoG+ cells, and impaired regeneration in PaskKO animals.

claim: PASK inhibition in ESCs and MuSCs increases the differentiation-capable progenitor population.
source: Using this system, we asked if PASKi treatment during the proliferative phase affects the expression of genes associated with stemness and self-renewal in cultured myoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data showing enrichment of stemness genes with PASKi treatment (Figure 1M).

claim: Global transcriptomic analysis revealed a strong enrichment of genes associated with stemness and self-renewal at all time-points when PASK is inhibited, starting with the proliferative condition.
source: Our global transcriptomic analysis revealed a strong enrichment of genes associated with stemness and self-renewal at all time-points when PASK is inhibited, starting with the proliferative condition (Figure 1M, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq heatmap and GSEA data in Figure 1M and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: PASK inhibition preserved self-renewal and stemness despite culture conditions that otherwise stimulate differentiation.
source: Furthermore, PASK inhibition preserved self-renewal and stemness despite culture conditions that otherwise stimulate differentiation (Figure 1M, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data showing maintained stemness gene expression in differentiating conditions with PASKi (Figure 1M, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).

claim: PASK inhibition is a viable strategy to preserve in vitro self-renewal and pluripotency of ESCs and adult stem cells.
source: Our results in ESCs and MuSCs show that the PASK inhibition is a viable strategy to preserve in vitro self-renewal and pluripotency of ESCs and adult stem cells and is indicative of its functional role in balancing stemness and pluripotency with differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations showing preserved stemness with PASKi in both ESCs and MuSCs.

claim: In proliferating C2C12 myoblasts (day 0), most of the PASK is localized in the cytosol and excluded from the nucleus.
source: In proliferating C2C12 myoblasts (day 0), most of the PASK is localized in the cytosol and excluded from the nucleus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: PASK appears to be localized into cytoplasmic granules in cultured myoblasts.
source: Curiously, PASK appears to be localized into cytoplasmic granules in cultured myoblasts (Figure 2A, inset).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing granular staining pattern in Figure 2A inset.

claim: Upon induction of the differentiation program, a significant loss of the cytoplasmic granular staining pattern occurs, and a large fraction of PASK was redistributed into the nucleus.
source: Upon induction of the differentiation program, a significant loss of the cytoplasmic granular staining pattern occurs, and a large fraction of PASK was redistributed into the nucleus, as seen by overlapping intensities of the PASK signal with the nuclear marker DAPI and by biochemical fractionation (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and biochemical fractionation data in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isolated primary myoblasts showed a strong granular staining pattern of PASK in proliferating myoblasts.
source: Similar to cultured myoblasts, isolated primary myoblasts showed a strong granular staining pattern of PASK in proliferating myoblasts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2C.

claim: Nearly all cells in which PASK was localized into the cytoplasmic granules were strongly positive for Pax7 expression.
source: Furthermore, nearly all cells in which PASK was localized into the cytoplasmic granules were strongly positive for Pax7 expression (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and violin plot data in Figure 2D.

claim: Cells with any extent of nuclear-localized PASK lacked Pax7 expression, even under proliferating conditions.
source: In contrast, cells with any extent of nuclear-localized PASK lacked Pax7 expression, even under proliferating conditions (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and violin plot data in Figure 2D.

claim: In nascent myotubes, the PASK localization pattern is switched from within cytoplasmic granules to diffused nuclear, which correlated with the loss of Pax7 positivity.
source: In addition, in nascent myotubes (Figure 2E, marked by arrow), the PASK localization pattern is switched from within cytoplasmic granules to diffused nuclear, which correlated with the loss of Pax7 positivity (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Nuclear translocation of PASK might be associated with heterogeneity in Pax7+ cell numbers seen in proliferating myoblasts.
source: These results suggest that nuclear translocation of PASK might be associated with heterogeneity in Pax7+ cell numbers seen in proliferating myoblasts (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between PASK localization and Pax7 expression shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Under proliferating conditions, Pax7hi cells are more frequently associated with cytoplasmic PASK presence.
source: Consistent with this, under proliferating conditions, Pax7hi (Figure 2G, yellow arrow indicates cells with stronger nuclear levels of Pax7) cells are more frequently associated with cytoplasmic PASK presence, and Pax7L0 (Figure 2G, white arrows indicate cells with relatively weaker nuclear levels of Pax7) or Pax7ab (cells lacking nuclear Pax7) are more frequently seen in cells with noticeable nuclear PASK presence (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Asymmetric nuclear distribution of PASK in rapidly dividing myoblasts creates heterogeneity in Pax7 expression, wherein a cell that asymmetrically retained nuclear PASK exhibited the loss of Pax7 expression post-mitosis.
source: Interestingly, we noticed asymmetric nuclear distribution of PASK in rapidly dividing myoblasts wherein a cell that asymmetrically retained nuclear PASK exhibited the loss of Pax7 expression post-mitosis, thereby creating heterogeneity in Pax7 expression in culture conditions (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing asymmetric PASK distribution and Pax7 loss in Figure 2I.

claim: There is a mechanistic connection between PASK nuclear translocation and heterogeneity in Pax7 expression in proliferating myoblasts.
source: Combined with data from Figure 1, our results indicated the mechanistic connection between PASK nuclear translocation and heterogeneity in Pax7 expression in proliferating myoblasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations linking PASK localization with Pax7 expression patterns.

claim: NLS-tagging was insufficient to drive PASK into the nucleus.
source: To our surprise, NLS-tagging was insufficient to drive PASK into the nucleus (Figure 3A), indicating the possible presence of a powerful nuclear export sequence (NES) in PASK that ensures cytoplasmic localization of PASK in proliferating cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A showing cytoplasmic localization of NLS-PASK.

claim: Treatment of cells expressing NLS-hPASK with leptomycin B (LMB) resulted in a modestly increased nuclear-localized PASK.
source: Consistent with this, treatment of cells expressing NLS-hPASK but not WT-hPASK with nuclear exportin 1 (CRM1) inhibitor, leptomycin B (LMB), resulted in a modestly increased nuclear-localized PASK (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A showing increased nuclear PASK with LMB treatment.

claim: Previous high-throughput studies have shown the interaction between human PASK and CRM1.
source: Previous high-throughput studies have shown the interaction between human PASK and CRM1 (Kırlı et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Kırlı et al., 2015).

claim: The GFP-WT-PASK (MW=~200 kDa) and GFP-1–737 (MW=~115 kDa) fragment remained predominantly cytoplasmic.
source: Scoring for cells showing at least some nuclear GFP presence, we found that the GFP-WT-PASK (MW=~200 kDa) and GFP-1–737 (MW=~115 kDa) fragment remained predominantly cytoplasmic (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3C showing cytoplasmic localization of these constructs.

claim: A smaller fragment, GFP-1–660 (MW=~100 kDa) showed nuclear GFP expression in ~22% of cells.
source: A smaller fragment, GFP-1–660 (MW=~100 kDa) showed nuclear GFP expression in ~22% of cells (Figure 3C), while fragment GFP-1–400 (MW=~70 kDa) showed increased nuclear localization of PASK with ~67% of cells showing at least some nuclear GFP presence (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 3C.

claim: Fragment GFP-1–400 (MW=~70 kDa) showed increased nuclear localization of PASK with ~67% of cells showing at least some nuclear GFP presence.
source: A smaller fragment, GFP-1–660 (MW=~100 kDa) showed nuclear GFP expression in ~22% of cells (Figure 3C), while fragment GFP-1–400 (MW=~70 kDa) showed increased nuclear localization of PASK with ~67% of cells showing at least some nuclear GFP presence (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 3C.

claim: There is a presence of NES between amino acids 400 and 660 and between amino acids 660 and 737 in PASK.
source: These results suggested the presence of NES between amino acids 400 and 660 and between amino acids 660 and 737.
evidence: This is an inference based on the truncation analysis data in Figure 3C.

claim: L401–L409 (NES1) and L666–L671 (NES2) are putative NES in PASK.
source: We used multiple bioinformatic tools to identify L401–L409 (NES1) and L666–L671 (NES2) as putative NES in PASK (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—source data 1 and 2; Xu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citations to bioinformatic tools (Xu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2021).

claim: The NES1 residues are similar to an experimentally verified NES in PGC1-α.
source: The NES1 residues are similar to an experimentally verified NES in PGC1-α (Chang et al., 2010), and the NES2 residues are similar to the NES of PDK1 that we previously discovered (Figure 3D; Lim et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment in Figure 3D and citations to prior work (Chang et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2003).

claim: The NES2 residues are similar to the NES of PDK1.
source: The NES1 residues are similar to an experimentally verified NES in PGC1-α (Chang et al., 2010), and the NES2 residues are similar to the NES of PDK1 that we previously discovered (Figure 3D; Lim et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment in Figure 3D and citation to prior work (Lim et al., 2003).

claim: Mutation of either NES1 or NES2 residues resulted in a modest but statistically significant increase in the number of cells with nuclear PASK localization compared to WT-PASK or NLS-PASK in the absence of LMB.
source: We found that mutation of either NES1 or NES2 residues resulted in a modest but statistically significant increase in the number of cells with nuclear PASK localization compared to WT-PASK or NLS-PASK in the absence of LMB (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 3E.

claim: Combined mutation of NES1 and NES2 resulted in a significantly increased proportion of cells that contain nuclear PASK.
source: Combined mutation of NES1 and NES2 resulted in a significantly increased proportion of cells that contain nuclear PASK, with the extent of nuclear PASK in each cell similar to what we observed for PASK during myogenesis (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 3E.

claim: Mutations of individual NES1 or NES2 in NLS-PASK improved nuclear retention of NLS-PASK.
source: Consistent with that, while mutations of individual NES1 or NES2 in NLS-PASK improved nuclear retention of NLS-PASK (Figure 3F), mutating both NES1 and NES2 together in NLS-PASK resulted in robust nuclear retention of NLS-PASK in nearly 100% of cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 3F.

claim: Mutating both NES1 and NES2 together in NLS-PASK resulted in robust nuclear retention of NLS-PASK in nearly 100% of cells.
source: Consistent with that, while mutations of individual NES1 or NES2 in NLS-PASK improved nuclear retention of NLS-PASK (Figure 3F), mutating both NES1 and NES2 together in NLS-PASK resulted in robust nuclear retention of NLS-PASK in nearly 100% of cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 3F.

claim: NES1 and NES2 are functional for exporting PASK from the nucleus, and their loss interferes with the nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling of PASK.
source: These results conclusively show that NES1 and NES2 are functional for exporting PASK from the nucleus, and their loss interferes with the nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling of PASK.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NES mutation data showing increased nuclear retention (Figure 3E-F).

claim: NLS-PASK was excluded from the nucleus in serum-starved cells despite LMB treatment.
source: Remarkably, NLS-PASK was excluded from the nucleus in serum-starved cells despite LMB treatment (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3G showing cytoplasmic NLS-PASK in serum-free conditions with LMB.

claim: Acute serum stimulation increased nuclear accumulation of NLS-PASK even without LMB.
source: In contrast, acute serum stimulation increased nuclear accumulation of NLS-PASK even without LMB (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3G showing nuclear NLS-PASK with serum stimulation.

claim: Serum stimulation improved the effectiveness of LMB treatment in blocking PASK nuclear export.
source: Furthermore, serum stimulation improved the effectiveness of LMB treatment, as seen from stronger nuclear retention of PASK (in nearly 100% of cells), similar to what was observed with NES1+NES2 mutated NLS-PASK.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3G showing increased nuclear retention with serum+LMB.

claim: Serum stimulation weakens the effectiveness of the NES1 and/or NES2 sequences to reduce the nuclear export rate of PASK.
source: The improved effectiveness of LMB in blocking PASK nuclear export suggests that serum stimulation weakens the effectiveness of the NES1 and/or NES2 sequences to reduce the nuclear export rate of PASK.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that serum+LMB is more effective than LMB alone (Figure 3G).

claim: Serum stimulation can trigger the nuclear translocation of endogenous and overexpressed GFP-tagged WT-PASK.
source: We next asked if serum stimulation can trigger the nuclear translocation of endogenous and overexpressed GFP-tagged WT-PASK. As shown in Figure 4A, we observed significant nuclear accumulation of GFP-hPASK by 2 hr of serum stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A showing nuclear GFP-PASK with serum stimulation.

claim: Endogenous mouse PASK was translocated to the nucleus in response to acute serum stimulation in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: In addition, endogenous mouse PASK was also translocated to the nucleus in response to acute serum stimulation in C2C12 myoblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PASK is phosphorylated and activated by mTORC1 in response to serum stimulation.
source: We have previously shown that PASK is phosphorylated and activated by mTORC1 in response to serum stimulation (Kikani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2019).

claim: Inhibiting mTORC1 by rapamycin did not consistently or significantly block serum-induced nuclear translocation of WT-hPASK.
source: However, inhibiting mTORC1 by rapamycin did not consistently or significantly block serum-induced nuclear translocation of WT-hPASK. This suggests that mTORC1 alone is insufficient for driving the nuclear translocation of PASK in response to serum stimulation (Figure 4A) and that a separate signaling input controls its nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A showing nuclear PASK with serum+rapamycin.

claim: mTORC1 alone is insufficient for driving the nuclear translocation of PASK in response to serum stimulation.
source: However, inhibiting mTORC1 by rapamycin did not consistently or significantly block serum-induced nuclear translocation of WT-hPASK. This suggests that mTORC1 alone is insufficient for driving the nuclear translocation of PASK in response to serum stimulation (Figure 4A) and that a separate signaling input controls its nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapamycin data in Figure 4A.

claim: Acetylation of non-histone proteins plays an important role in controlling nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling and cell fate decisions in stem cells.
source: Along with phosphorylation, acetylation of non-histone proteins plays an important role in controlling nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling and cell fate decisions in stem cells (Choudhary et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Choudhary et al., 2014).

claim: Endogenous PASK is acetylated in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: To determine if endogenous PASK is acetylated, we treated C2C12 myoblasts with trichostatin A, a broad-spectrum histone deacetylase inhibitor. Probing the purified acetylome with an anti-PASK antibody revealed strong enrichment of acetylated endogenous mouse PASK (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is a dose and time-dependent increase in PASK acetylation caused by serum stimulation in HEK293T cells.
source: We also noticed a dose (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and time-dependent (Figure 4B) increase in PASK acetylation caused by serum stimulation in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A significant fraction of mouse PASK is acetylated during regeneration on days 3 and 5 post-injury.
source: To examine the physiological relevance of PASK acetylation in vivo, we injured mouse tibialis anterior (TA) muscles and analyzed PASK acetylation on day 3 and day 5 post-injury. We noticed that a significant fraction of mouse PASK is acetylated during regeneration on days 3 and 5 post-injury (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data from injured muscle tissue in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PASK is a novel non-histone protein target of signal-dependent acetylation in cells and tissues.
source: Together, these results show that PASK is a novel non-histone protein target of signal-dependent acetylation in cells and tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations of PASK acetylation in cells and tissues.

claim: Kat2a and EP300 are two major histone acetyltransferases upregulated in MuSCs during regeneration.
source: Kat2a and EP300 are two major histone acetyltransferases upregulated in MuSCs during regeneration and are known to induce the acetylation of non-histone proteins during myogenesis (Das et al., 2017; Puri et al., 1997a; Puri et al., 1997b; Sartorelli et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Das et al., 2017; Puri et al., 1997a; Puri et al., 1997b; Sartorelli et al., 1999).

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of Kat2a did not affect serum-induced acetylation of PASK.
source: siRNA-mediated knockdown of Kat2a did not affect serum-induced acetylation of PASK (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Pretreatment of cells with CBP/P300 inhibitor A-485 nearly completely blocked serum-induced PASK acetylation.
source: In contrast, the pretreatment of cells with a highly selective CBP/P300 inhibitor, A-485 (Lasko et al., 2017), nearly completely blocked serum-induced PASK acetylation (Figure 4C) in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4C and citation to the A-485 inhibitor (Lasko et al., 2017).

claim: Knockdown of EP300 in C2C12 cells completely inhibited endogenous PASK acetylation induced by serum.
source: Furthermore, the knockdown of EP300 in C2C12 cells completely inhibited endogenous PASK acetylation induced by serum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Serum-induced PASK nuclear localization was blocked by the pretreatment of cells with A-485.
source: Finally, serum-induced PASK nuclear localization (Figure 4D) was blocked by the pretreatment of cells with A-485.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4D showing cytoplasmic PASK with A-485 treatment.

claim: PASK is a novel acetylation target of CBP/EP300 that drives its nuclear translocation in response to serum stimulation.
source: Thus, PASK is a novel acetylation target of CBP/EP300 that drives its nuclear translocation in response to serum stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing CBP/EP300-dependent PASK acetylation and nuclear translocation (Figure 4C-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Serum-induced PASK acetylation was independent of inputs from signaling kinases PI-3K, mTOR, or Akt.
source: However, serum-induced PASK acetylation was independent of inputs from signaling kinases, as inhibition of PI-3K, mTOR, or Akt did not prevent serum-induced PASK acetylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Inhibition of the mitochondrial pyruvate complex (MPC1) by UK5099 stimulated PASK acetylation more than serum alone.
source: Strikingly, inhibition of the mitochondrial pyruvate complex (MPC1) by UK5099 stimulated PASK acetylation more than serum alone, perhaps due to a compensatory increase in glutaminolysis (Figure 4F; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4F and citation to prior work on compensatory glutaminolysis (Yang et al., 2014).

claim: Inhibition of mitochondrial glutaminolysis by GLS1-specific inhibitor BPTES resulted in a near-complete loss of serum-induced PASK acetylation.
source: Consistent with this, inhibition of mitochondrial glutaminolysis by a GLS1-specific inhibitor, BPTES, resulted in a near-complete loss of serum-induced PASK acetylation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4F.

claim: Glutamine added back to cells cultured in glutamine- and serum-free media conditions was sufficient to stimulate PASK acetylation as much as serum induction.
source: Furthermore, only glutamine added back to cells cultured in glutamine- and serum-free media conditions was sufficient to stimulate PASK acetylation as much as serum induction (Figure 4G), which was further inhibited by BPTES (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4G.

claim: Glutamine metabolism drives PASK acetylation via CBP/P300.
source: Finally, glutamine metabolism drives PASK acetylation via CBP/P300 since pretreatment of serum-stimulated cells with BPTES or glutamine-stimulated cells with the A-485 markedly blunted the PASK acetylation in isolated primary MuSCs (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data in Figure 4H.

claim: Glutamine starvation resulted in the nuclear exclusion of PASK.
source: As shown in Figure 4I, glutamine starvation resulted in the nuclear exclusion of PASK.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4I showing cytoplasmic PASK with glutamine starvation.

claim: Glutamine addition alone in serum- and glutamine-free media stimulated robust nuclear translocation of PASK.
source: On the other hand, glutamine addition alone in serum- and glutamine-free media stimulated robust nuclear translocation of PASK, which was blocked by CBP/EP300 inhibition (A-485), but not by mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4I showing nuclear PASK with glutamine stimulation.

claim: Glutamine-induced nuclear translocation of PASK was blocked by CBP/EP300 inhibition (A-485), but not by mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin.
source: On the other hand, glutamine addition alone in serum- and glutamine-free media stimulated robust nuclear translocation of PASK, which was blocked by CBP/EP300 inhibition (A-485), but not by mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4I showing cytoplasmic PASK with A-485 but nuclear PASK with rapamycin.

claim: Glutamine signaling to CBP/EP300, but not to mTOR, regulates PASK nuclear translocation via acetylation.
source: Thus, our results show that glutamine signaling to CBP/EP300, but not to mTOR, regulates PASK nuclear translocation via acetylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing glutamine-dependent, CBP/EP300-mediated, mTOR-independent PASK acetylation and nuclear translocation (Figure 4G-I).

claim: Glutamine withdrawal significantly reduced the proliferation rate of cultured myoblasts.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Shang et al., 2020; Ahsan et al., 2020), glutamine withdrawal significantly reduced the proliferation rate of cultured myoblasts (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 5A and citations to prior literature (Shang et al., 2020; Ahsan et al., 2020).

claim: Glutamine-withdrawn cells were greatly enlarged and remained alive in cell culture for at least 4 days.
source: However, the glutamine-withdrawn cells were greatly enlarged and remained alive in cell culture for at least 4 days (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Cells grown in glutamine-replete media exhibited a lower proportion of Pax7+ myoblasts.
source: Furthermore, cells grown in glutamine-replete media exhibited a lower proportion of Pax7+ myoblasts, consistent with a previous report (Olguin and Olwin, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5B-C and citation to prior work (Olguin and Olwin, 2004).

claim: Acute glutamine withdrawal resulted in a significantly reduced heterogeneity in Pax7 expression due to a significant increase in the percentage of Pax7+ myoblasts.
source: Interestingly, acute glutamine withdrawal resulted in a significantly reduced heterogeneity in Pax7 expression due to a significant increase in the percentage of Pax7+ myoblasts (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Isolated primary myoblasts cells grown in glutamine-replete media exhibited a decreased proportion of Pax7+ myoblasts.
source: Consistent with results from cultured myoblasts, isolated primary myoblasts cells grown in glutamine-replete media exhibited a decreased proportion of Pax7+ myoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Glutamine-depleted primary myoblasts showed a marked increase in the percent Pax7+ myoblasts, resulting in reduced myoblast heterogeneity in terms of Pax7 expression.
source: In contrast, glutamine-depleted cells showed a marked increase in the percent Pax7+ myoblasts, resulting in reduced myoblast heterogeneity in terms of Pax7 expression (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: There is a connection between glutamine metabolism and MuSCs heterogeneity via regulation of Pax7 expression dynamics.
source: These results suggest a connection between glutamine metabolism and MuSCs heterogeneity via regulation of Pax7 expression dynamics, warranting further mechanistic investigation.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations linking glutamine availability with Pax7 expression heterogeneity (Figure 5B-E).

claim: BrdU+ cells (proliferating cells) in glutamine-rich media were smaller in size and displayed heterogeneity in the level of nuclear Pax7 expression.
source: BrdU+ cells (proliferating cells) in glutamine-rich media were smaller in size and displayed heterogeneity in the level of nuclear Pax7 expression (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation and Pax7 immunofluorescence data in Figure 5F-G.

claim: There was a significant Pax7L0 and Pax7ab population among the BrdU+ cycling stem cells grown in glutamine-replete media.
source: We also noticed a significant Pax7L0 and Pax7ab population among the BrdU+ cycling stem cells grown in glutamine-replete media (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation and Pax7 immunofluorescence data in Figure 5F-G.

claim: Glutamine withdrawal blunted BrdU incorporation yet resulted in a robust increase in the proportion of Pax7hi cells due to increased Pax7 staining intensity within individual cells.
source: In contrast, glutamine withdrawal blunted BrdU incorporation yet resulted in a robust increase in the proportion of Pax7hi cells due to increased Pax7 staining intensity within individual cells (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation and Pax7 immunofluorescence data in Figure 5F-H.

claim: The ratio of Pax7+/BrdU+ nuclei is increased by glutamine withdrawal.
source: Since the ratio of Pax7+/BrdU+ nuclei is increased by glutamine withdrawal (Figure 5H), our results indicate that glutamine withdrawal results in a reactivation of Pax7 expression in Pax7lo MuSCs in the absence of cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5H.

claim: Glutamine withdrawal results in a reactivation of Pax7 expression in Pax7lo MuSCs in the absence of cell proliferation.
source: Since the ratio of Pax7+/BrdU+ nuclei is increased by glutamine withdrawal (Figure 5H), our results indicate that glutamine withdrawal results in a reactivation of Pax7 expression in Pax7lo MuSCs in the absence of cell proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased Pax7+/BrdU+ ratio with glutamine withdrawal (Figure 5H).

claim: Pax7 mRNA levels were significantly increased when glutamine was withdrawn, whereas mRNA levels for proliferation marker MKi67 were nearly completely blunted.
source: Consistent with this, Pax7 mRNA levels were significantly increased when glutamine was withdrawn, whereas mRNA levels for proliferation marker MKi67 were nearly completely blunted (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transcript levels of uncommitted myoblast markers, such as Cd34, Myf5, and Myod1, were significantly elevated upon glutamine deprivation.
source: In addition to Pax7, transcript levels of uncommitted myoblast markers, such as Cd34, Myf5, and Myod1, were also significantly elevated upon glutamine deprivation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was a significant increase in the expression of Foxo3, a marker for MuSC quiescence, upon glutamine withdrawal.
source: We also noticed a significant increase in the expression of Foxo3, a marker for MuSC quiescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), perhaps reflective of reduced proliferation due to glutamine withdrawal.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Glutamine withdrawal enforces the stemness preservation program and induces quiescence in vitro in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: These results suggested that glutamine withdrawal enforces the stemness preservation program and induces quiescence in vitro in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on increased stemness markers and quiescence markers with glutamine withdrawal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Glutamine withdrawal resulted in a near-complete loss of Myog.
source: Finally, glutamine withdrawal also resulted in a near-complete loss of Myog, indicating a dependence on glutamine metabolism to generate the committed progenitor population (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Glutamine depletion blocked myogenesis.
source: We validated these functions of glutamine in cultured myoblasts as glutamine withdrawal or inhibition of Gls1 by BPTES treatment increased Pax7 mRNA levels in C2C12 myoblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). While glutamine depletion blocked myogenesis, inhibition of mitochondrial pyruvate import by UK5099 strongly stimulated differentiation as measured by Myog, Mylpf, and Acta1 transcript levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and immunostaining (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), perhaps via increased glutaminolysis (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Inhibition of mitochondrial pyruvate import by UK5099 strongly stimulated differentiation as measured by Myog, Mylpf, and Acta1 transcript levels and immunostaining.
source: While glutamine depletion blocked myogenesis, inhibition of mitochondrial pyruvate import by UK5099 strongly stimulated differentiation as measured by Myog, Mylpf, and Acta1 transcript levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and immunostaining (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), perhaps via increased glutaminolysis (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C and citation to prior work on compensatory glutaminolysis (Yang et al., 2014).

claim: During the early muscle regeneration response, glutamine, enriched in the regenerating niche, is taken up by activated MuSCs, which drives their proliferation and is required for myogenic commitment and the regenerative myogenesis program.
source: During the early muscle regeneration response, glutamine, enriched in the regenerating niche, is taken up by activated MuSCs, which drives their proliferation and is required for myogenic commitment and the regenerative myogenesis program (Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Shang et al., 2020).

claim: A quiescent, self-renewing population is established after the early wave of the myogenesis program has largely concluded (days 5–7 post-injury).
source: According to a recent report, a quiescent, self-renewing population is established after this early wave of the myogenesis program has largely concluded (days 5–7 post-injury) (Cutler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Cutler et al., 2021).

claim: After early myogenesis, 3 days of BPTES treatment did not appear to affect regenerative myofiber sizes.
source: After early myogenesis, 3 days of BPTES treatment did not appear to affect regenerative myofiber sizes (laminin A staining, Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by laminin staining data in Figure 5J.

claim: There was a significant increase in Pax7+ cell numbers in BPTES-treated compared with DMSO-treated animals after 3 days of treatment following early myogenesis.
source: In contrast, we saw a significant increase in Pax7+ cell numbers in BPTES-treated compared with DMSO-treated animals (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: This is supported by Pax7 immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 5J-K.

claim: Compared with proliferating cells, early differentiating myoblasts show significantly increased intracellular glutamine levels and their associated downstream metabolites, glutamate, alpha-ketoglutarate, and aspartate.
source: Compared with proliferating cells, early differentiating myoblasts show significantly increased intracellular glutamine levels and their associated downstream metabolites, glutamate, alpha-ketoglutarate, and aspartate (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics volcano plot data in Figure 5L.

claim: Under glutamine-depleted conditions where proliferation is inhibited but stemness is enhanced, there was a significant reduction in alpha-ketoglutarate, citrate, and malate levels.
source: Under glutamine-depleted conditions where proliferation is inhibited but stemness is enhanced (Figure 5F–H), we noticed a significant reduction in alpha-ketoglutarate, citrate, and malate levels, indicating a possible reliance on reductive carboxylation from alpha-ketoglutarate in proliferative myoblasts (Figure 5L–N, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 5L-N and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: The addition of cell-permeable alpha-ketoglutarate reversed the increased Pax7+ cell numbers in glutamine-depleted culture conditions.
source: Consistent with this, the addition of cell-permeable alpha-ketoglutarate reversed the increased Pax7+ cell numbers in glutamine-depleted culture conditions (Figure 5O–P).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 5O-P.

claim: Glutamine metabolism links proliferation with the passage from Pax7hi stem cells to Pax7L0/Ab progenitors, progressively establishing a commitment to differentiate (MyoG+).
source: Taken together, our results suggest that glutamine metabolism links proliferation with the passage from Pax7hi stem cells to Pax7L0/Ab progenitors, progressively establishing a commitment to differentiate (MyoG+).
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations linking glutamine metabolism with Pax7 expression dynamics and differentiation.

claim: Unlike glutamine withdrawal, PASK inhibition did not affect cell proliferation rate or size in isolated MuSCs.
source: Unlike glutamine withdrawal, PASK inhibition did not affect cell proliferation rate or size (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) in isolated MuSCs.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Similar to glutamine withdrawal, PASK inhibition significantly increased Pax7+ myoblast numbers and reduced the heterogeneity of Pax7 nuclear-staining intensities across the field in isolated MuSCs.
source: Nevertheless, similar to glutamine withdrawal, PASK inhibition significantly increased Pax7+ myoblast numbers and reduced the heterogeneity of Pax7 nuclear-staining intensities across the field in isolated MuSCs (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 6A-B.

claim: PASK plays a specific role downstream of glutamine metabolism in regulating the self-renewal program but not cell proliferation machinery.
source: These results suggest that PASK plays a specific role downstream of glutamine metabolism in regulating the self-renewal program but not cell proliferation machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that PASKi affects Pax7 expression but not proliferation (Figure 6A-B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: PASKi treatment resulted in increased Pax7+ MuSCs numbers without affecting BrdU incorporation.
source: Interestingly, while PASKi did not affect BrdU incorporation, PASKi treatment resulted in increased Pax7+ MuSCs numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation and Pax7 immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: PASK selectively regulates the stemness downstream of glutamine metabolism without affecting the proliferation rate.
source: Thus, PASK selectively regulates the stemness downstream of glutamine metabolism without affecting the proliferation rate.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing PASKi affects Pax7 but not BrdU incorporation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C).

claim: PaskKO mice showed elevated Pax7+ MuSCs numbers even 14 days after injury, whereas Pax7+ MuSCs numbers decline in PaskWT muscles during that time.
source: Interestingly, as with acute Gls1 inhibition (Figure 5J–K), PaskKO mice showed elevated Pax7+ MuSCs numbers even 14 days after injury, whereas Pax7+ MuSCs numbers decline in PaskWT muscles during that time (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Pax7 immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 6C-D.

claim: PaskKO animals showed smaller myofiber fiber cross-sectional areas at 14 dpi compared with PaskWT muscle sections.
source: Furthermore, PaskKO animals showed smaller myofiber fiber cross-sectional areas at 14 dpi compared with PaskWT muscle sections (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by myofiber cross-sectional area quantification data in Figure 6E.

claim: Genetic loss or inhibition of PASK results in an increased proportion of Pax7+ myoblast numbers in vitro, expansion of Pax7+ MuSC numbers during muscle regeneration, and a compromised muscle regeneration response.
source: Thus, genetic loss or inhibition of PASK results in an increased proportion of Pax7+ myoblast numbers in vitro, expansion of Pax7+ MuSC numbers during muscle regeneration, and a compromised muscle regeneration response.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations in PaskKO and PASKi-treated cells and animals.

claim: The requirement of alpha-ketoglutarate as a co-factor in DNA and histone demethylation reactions is associated with its function in regulating cell fate in ESCs.
source: The requirement of alpha-ketoglutarate as a co-factor in DNA and histone demethylation reactions is associated with its function in regulating cell fate in ESCs (Ryall et al., 2015; TeSlaa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Ryall et al., 2015; TeSlaa et al., 2016).

claim: PASK inhibition rendered alpha-ketoglutarate ineffective in reducing Pax7+ stem cell numbers in glutamine-depleted media conditions.
source: Interestingly, PASK inhibition rendered alpha-ketoglutarate ineffective in reducing Pax7+ stem cell numbers in glutamine-depleted media conditions (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 6F-G.

claim: The glutamine-dependent nuclear translocation of PASK is an additional pathway that drives myoblast exit from self-renewal.
source: These results suggest that the glutamine-dependent nuclear translocation of PASK is an additional pathway that drives myoblast exit from self-renewal.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing that PASKi blocks the effect of alpha-ketoglutarate on Pax7 expression (Figure 6F-G).

claim: Glutamine depletion results in increased cytoplasmic retention of PASK in isolated myoblasts, with a concomitant increase in Pax7+ myoblasts.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we show that glutamine depletion results in increased cytoplasmic retention of PASK in isolated myoblasts, with a concomitant increase in Pax7+ myoblasts (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and violin plot data in Figure 6H-I.

claim: Glutamine metabolism targets PASK subcellular distribution to generate a Pax7-negative population.
source: Thus, we propose that glutamine metabolism targets PASK subcellular distribution to generate a Pax7-negative population.
evidence: This is an inference based on data linking glutamine metabolism with PASK nuclear translocation and Pax7 downregulation.

claim: An increase in Pax7+ cell numbers observed due to PASK silencing in cultured myoblasts could be reversed by the expression of either WT or nuclear hPASK (nPASK).
source: Consistent with this, an increase in Pax7+ cell numbers observed due to PASK silencing in cultured myoblasts could be reversed by the expression of either WT or nuclear hPASK (nPASK [NLS-PASK-NES1+2-GFP], Figure 6J–K), but not by GFP control (Figure 6J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 6J-K.

claim: Only nuclear PASK effectively reversed the increased Pax7+ myoblasts numbers due to glutamine depletion.
source: In contrast, only nuclear PASK effectively reversed the increased Pax7+ myoblasts numbers due to glutamine depletion (Figure 6L–M).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 6L-M.

claim: PASK is a downstream target of glutamine metabolism in activated myoblasts that counters Pax7 expression.
source: Taken together, we conclude that PASK is a downstream target of glutamine metabolism in activated myoblasts that counters Pax7 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations linking glutamine metabolism, PASK nuclear translocation, and Pax7 downregulation.

claim: There is an increased association between PASK and WDR5 at the onset of differentiation.
source: We have previously reported an increased association between PASK and WDR5, a member of the histone H3 lysine 4 methyltransferase complex at the onset of differentiation (Kikani et al., 2016; Karakkat et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kikani et al., 2016; Karakkat et al., 2019).

claim: WDR5 interacts with Pax7 and epigenetically maintains myoblast self-renewal.
source: Furthermore, WDR5 interacts with Pax7 and epigenetically maintains myoblast self-renewal (McKinnell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (McKinnell et al., 2008).

claim: Multiple alignments identified R942 as a conserved residue within the WIN motif that interacts directly with WDR5.
source: The multiple alignments identified R942 as a conserved residue within the WIN motif that interacts directly with WDR5 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 7A.

claim: Mutation of Arg942Gly (R942G) within the WIN motif ablated the interaction between hPASK and Flag-tagged mouse WDR5.
source: Mutation of Arg942Gly (R942G) within the WIN motif ablated the interaction between hPASK and Flag-tagged mouse WDR5 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7B.

claim: mTOR phosphorylates PASK at multiple sites to promote the PASK-WDR5 association.
source: We have previously reported that mTOR phosphorylates PASK at multiple sites to promote the PASK-WDR5 association (Kikani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2019).

claim: Phosphomimetic mutation of Ser949 to glutamic acid (E) resulted in a stronger association between PASK and WDR5.
source: Phosphomimetic mutation of a single mTOR phosphorylation site, Ser949 to glutamic acid (E), resulted in a stronger association between PASK and WDR5 (Figure 7B), further confirming that nutrient signaling modulates the PASK-WDR5 interaction (Kikani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7B and citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2019).

claim: WDR5 interacts with APC/C via a WIN motif during mitosis, and this interaction is required for the rapid transcriptional reactivation of self-renewal and lineage commitment genes following mitosis in ESCs.
source: In stem cells, WDR5 is reported to interact with the cell cycle-linked E3 ubiquitin ligase, APC/C via a WIN motif. This interaction is strengthened during mitosis and is required for the rapid transcriptional reactivation of self-renewal and lineage commitment genes following mitosis in ESCs (Oh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Oh et al., 2020).

claim: Disruption of the WDR5-APC/C interaction reduces stem cell pluripotency.
source: Disruption of the WDR5-APC/C interaction reduces stem cell pluripotency.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Oh et al., 2020) mentioned in the context.

claim: Human PASK rapidly enters the nucleus during mitosis, prior to nuclear membrane breakdown.
source: We have noticed rapid nuclear entry of human PASK during mitosis, prior to nuclear membrane breakdown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: APC2 is the only APC/C complex member that binds directly with WDR5 when the proteins are purified in vitro.
source: Since APC2 was demonstrated to be the only APC/C complex member that binds directly with WDR5 when the proteins are purified in vitro (Oh et al., 2020), we focused our co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiments on APC2 and CDC20, two members of the endogenous APC/C complex that interact with WDR5 during mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Oh et al., 2020).

claim: The presence of WT-PASK significantly disrupted WDR5-APC/C, as indicated by reduced co-precipitation of WDR5 with APC2 and CDC20 compared with control cells.
source: The presence of WT-PASK significantly disrupted WDR5-APC/C, as indicated by reduced co-precipitation of WDR5 with APC2 and CDC20 compared with control cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7C.

claim: PASKWIN mutant significantly strengthened the WDR5-APC/C interaction.
source: PASKWIN mutant, on the other hand, significantly strengthened the WDR5-APC/C interaction, suggesting that the interaction of PASK with WDR5 disrupts the WDR5-APC/C interaction (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7C.

claim: Co-expression of WT-PASK with WDR5 significantly reduced the WDR5-APC/C interaction during mitosis.
source: As shown in Figure 7D, co-expression of WT-PASK with WDR5 significantly reduced the WDR5-APC/C interaction.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from mitotic cells in Figure 7D.

claim: Co-expression of either kinase-dead (K1028R) or WIN mutant (R942G) PASK resulted in strengthened WDR5-APC/C interaction when compared to the expression of WT PASK.
source: However, co-expression of either kinase-dead (K1028R) or WIN mutant (R942G) PASK resulted in strengthened WDR5-APC/C interaction when compared to the expression of WT PASK (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from mitotic cells in Figure 7D.

claim: Expression of PASKS949E further reduced the WDR5-APC/C interaction compared with WT-PASK.
source: Expression of PASKS949E, on the other hand, further reduced the WDR5-APC/C interaction compared with WT-PASK, consistent with the stronger PASK-WDR5 association and increased PASK activity resulting from phosphorylation at the Ser949 site (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from mitotic cells in Figure 7D.

claim: PASK phosphorylated WDR5 at S49 and the phosphomimetic mutant of WDR5, S49E, dramatically reduced Pax7 expression and induced precocious myogenesis under proliferating conditions.
source: We previously showed that PASK phosphorylated WDR5 at S49 and that the phosphomimetic mutant of WDR5, S49E, dramatically reduced Pax7 expression and induced precocious myogenesis under proliferating conditions (Kikani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Kikani et al., 2016).

claim: WDR5S49E completely disrupted the WDR5-APC/C interaction during mitosis.
source: Interestingly, we find that WDR5S49E completely disrupted the WDR5-APC/C interaction during mitosis, suggesting that the catalytic function of PASK regulates the WDR5-APC/C interaction (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from mitotic cells in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Acute glutamine stimulation strengthened the PASK-WDR5 interaction in proliferating myoblasts.
source: Consistent with this, acute glutamine stimulation strengthened the PASK-WDR5 interaction in proliferating myoblasts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PASKi treatment strengthened the WDR5-APC/C interaction in glutamine-containing media during mitosis.
source: As shown in Figure 7F, PASKi treatment strengthened the WDR5-APC/C interaction in glutamine-containing media during mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from mitotic cells in Figure 7F.

claim: Glutamine withdrawal during mitosis was sufficient to strengthen the WDR5-APC/C interaction, and the addition of PASKi in the glutamine-depleted condition did not have further additive effects.
source: Interestingly, glutamine withdrawal during mitosis was sufficient to strengthen the WDR5-APC/C interaction, and the addition of PASKi in the glutamine-depleted condition did not have further additive effects (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from mitotic cells in Figure 7F.

claim: The WDR5-APC/C interaction is a target of glutamine metabolism during mitosis in stem cells and PASK relays the glutamine signaling to WDR5-APC/C.
source: This result suggests that the WDR5-APC/C interaction is a target of glutamine metabolism during mitosis in stem cells and that PASK relays the glutamine signaling to WDR5-APC/C.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing glutamine-dependent, PASK-mediated regulation of WDR5-APC/C interaction (Figure 7F).

claim: APC/C inhibition using the specific inhibitor proTAME resulted in a significant reduction in the number of Pax7+ cells after at least one round of the cell cycle (30 hr of treatment) compared with control cells.
source: Strikingly, APC/C inhibition using the specific inhibitor proTAME resulted in a significant reduction in the number of Pax7+ cells after at least one round of the cell cycle (30 hr of treatment) compared with control cells (Figure 7G–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 7G-H.

claim: PASKi treatment significantly increased Pax7+ cell number within 30 hr of treatment.
source: Within this timeframe, PASKi treatment significantly increased Pax7+ cell number (Figure 7G–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 7G-H.

claim: WT-PASK effectively downregulated Pax7 expression.
source: Additionally, WT-PASK effectively downregulated Pax7 expression (Figure 7I–J) while mutation of WIN (R942G), which abolishes the PASK-WDR5 interaction and strengthened WDR5-APC/C interaction, resulted in a near-complete failure in suppressing Pax7 expression with both WT and nuclear versions of PASK (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 7I-J.

claim: Mutation of WIN (R942G), which abolishes the PASK-WDR5 interaction and strengthened WDR5-APC/C interaction, resulted in a near-complete failure in suppressing Pax7 expression with both WT and nuclear versions of PASK.
source: Additionally, WT-PASK effectively downregulated Pax7 expression (Figure 7I–J) while mutation of WIN (R942G), which abolishes the PASK-WDR5 interaction and strengthened WDR5-APC/C interaction, resulted in a near-complete failure in suppressing Pax7 expression with both WT and nuclear versions of PASK (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7I.

claim: Acute inhibition of APC/C resulted in the transcriptional induction of the committed progenitor and differentiation markers, Myog and Mylpf, respectively.
source: Finally, acute inhibition of APC/C resulted in the transcriptional induction of the committed progenitor and differentiation markers, Myog and Mylpf, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Inhibition of WDR5 or PASK, alone or in combination with APC/C inhibitor, prevented the establishment of the committed progenitor population and blocked differentiation.
source: In contrast, inhibition of WDR5 or PASK, alone or in combination with APC/C inhibitor, prevented the establishment of the committed progenitor population and blocked differentiation (Figure 7G–H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and RT-qPCR data in Figure 7G-H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PASK and WDR5 have multifaceted functions that act in conjunction with APC/C to regulate the generation of committed progenitors.
source: These results suggest multifaceted functions of PASK and WDR5 that act in conjunction with APC/C to regulate the generation of committed progenitors and indicate that proper temporal transition of cell identity is required for successful terminal differentiation.
