evidence: This is an inference based on data showing complex interactions between PASK, WDR5, and APC/C in regulating differentiation.

claim: Proper temporal transition of cell identity is required for successful terminal differentiation.
source: These results suggest multifaceted functions of PASK and WDR5 that act in conjunction with APC/C to regulate the generation of committed progenitors and indicate that proper temporal transition of cell identity is required for successful terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that disrupting the PASK-WDR5-APC/C axis blocks differentiation.

claim: PASK is a novel signaling kinase that connects glutamine metabolism with the WDR5-APC/C complex interaction to control stem cell fate.
source: Therefore, we provide a novel signaling role of PASK in connecting glutamine metabolism with the WDR5-APC/C complex interaction to control stem cell fate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comprehensive data linking glutamine metabolism, PASK acetylation/nuclear translocation, and WDR5-APC/C disruption.

claim: The proliferative functions of glutamine metabolism are co-opted by stem cells to establish stem cell fate via PASK in response to the changing metabolic landscape.
source: Our results suggest that the proliferative functions of glutamine metabolism are co-opted by stem cells to establish stem cell fate via PASK in response to the changing metabolic landscape.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comprehensive findings linking glutamine metabolism with PASK-mediated regulation of stem cell fate.

claim: PASK is a novel sensory kinase that integrates hormonal (via mTOR) and metabolic signals (via glutamine) into the post-mitotic machinery to counter the reestablishment of stem cell identity.
source: Through comprehensive studies in this manuscript, we identify PASK as a novel sensory kinase that integrates hormonal (via mTOR) and metabolic signals (via glutamine) into the post-mitotic machinery to counter the reestablishment of stem cell identity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comprehensive data showing PASK responds to both mTOR and glutamine signals to regulate stem cell fate.

claim: Glutamine stimulates the proliferation of activated myoblasts to bring activated stem cells into mitosis.
source: Our data support a model where glutamine stimulates the proliferation of activated myoblasts to bring activated stem cells into mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by data showing glutamine is required for proliferation (Figure 5A) and prior literature (Shang et al., 2020).

claim: Glutamine induces concomitant acetylation of PASK to drive its nuclear translocation and guide the exit from self-renewal, establishing the committed progenitor pool during early muscle regeneration.
source: Furthermore, glutamine induces concomitant acetylation of PASK to drive its nuclear translocation and guide the exit from self-renewal, establishing the committed progenitor pool during early muscle regeneration (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data showing glutamine-dependent PASK acetylation (Figure 4G-I), nuclear translocation (Figure 4I), and regulation of Pax7 expression (Figure 5B-E, 6H-I).

claim: As a metabolic sensory kinase enriched in stem cells, PASK functions to integrate metabolic (via glutamine) and nutrient signaling (via mTOR) inputs to orchestrate exit from self-renewal and promote the onset of the terminal differentiation program.
source: Thus, as a metabolic sensory kinase enriched in stem cells, PASK functions to integrate metabolic (via glutamine) and nutrient signaling (via mTOR) inputs to orchestrate exit from self-renewal and promote the onset of the terminal differentiation program.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comprehensive findings showing PASK responds to both glutamine and mTOR signals to regulate differentiation.

claim: PASK subcellular localization in stem cells must be carefully regulated to prevent unintended differentiation.
source: Our data suggest that PASK subcellular localization in stem cells must be carefully regulated to prevent unintended differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing nuclear PASK drives differentiation while cytoplasmic PASK maintains stemness.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of PASK is signal-regulated.
source: In agreement, our results indicate that nuclear accumulation of PASK is signal-regulated.
evidence: This is supported by data showing serum and glutamine regulate PASK nuclear translocation (Figure 3G, 4A, 4I).

claim: Serum-induced PASK nuclear localization was independent of mTOR but dependent upon CBP/P300-induced acetylation.
source: Serum-induced PASK nuclear localization was independent of mTOR but dependent upon CBP/P300-induced acetylation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing rapamycin doesn't block PASK nuclear translocation (Figure 4A) but A-485 does (Figure 4D).

claim: CBP/P300 has been reported to acetylate other non-histone proteins, mainly transcription regulatory factors, during myogenesis.
source: Interestingly, CBP/P300 has been reported to other acetylate non-histone proteins, mainly transcription regulatory factors, during myogenesis (Puri et al., 1997a; Puri et al., 1997b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Puri et al., 1997a; Puri et al., 1997b).

claim: PASK is a novel kinase target of CBP/P300 in MuSCs that drives differentiation by coordinating exit from self-renewal.
source: Our results suggest that PASK is a novel kinase target of CBP/P300 in MuSCs that drives differentiation by coordinating exit from self-renewal.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing CBP/P300-dependent PASK acetylation drives nuclear translocation and differentiation.

claim: Mitochondrial glutamine metabolism is the primary source of acetyl-CoA for driving both PASK acetylation and nuclear translocation.
source: Our data conclusively shows that mitochondrial glutamine metabolism is the primary source of acetyl-coA for driving both PASK acetylation and nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing BPTES blocks PASK acetylation (Figure 4F-H) and nuclear translocation (Figure 4I).

claim: Glutamine is a major fuel early during the myogenesis program, which coincides with the temporal point at which PASK expression is at its highest in regenerating muscles.
source: Furthermore, glutamine is a major fuel early during the myogenesis program, which coincides with the temporal point at which PASK expression is at its highest in regenerating muscles (Kikani et al., 2016; Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kikani et al., 2016; Shang et al., 2020).

claim: Increased glutamine influx from the regenerating niche induces PASK acetylation and nuclear translocation to promote the onset of the myogenesis program early during regeneration.
source: Thus, we propose that increased glutamine influx from the regenerating niche induces PASK acetylation and nuclear translocation to promote the onset of the myogenesis program early during regeneration.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the temporal correlation between glutamine availability, PASK expression, and myogenesis.

claim: Glutamine and PASK act on the same downstream mechanisms to regulate self-renewal.
source: These data suggest that glutamine and PASK act on the same downstream mechanisms to regulate self-renewal.
evidence: This is an inference based on similar phenotypes observed with glutamine withdrawal and PASK inhibition.

claim: WDR5 is required to maintain self-renewal in ESCs and adult MuSCs via its association with Oct4 and Pax7 transcription factors, respectively.
source: Furthermore, WDR5 is required to maintain self-renewal in ESCs and adult MuSCs via its association with Oct4 and Pax7 transcription factors, respectively (McKinnell et al., 2008; Ang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (McKinnell et al., 2008; Ang et al., 2011).

claim: WDR5 serves as a substrate adaptor by associating with APC/C during mitosis to ubiquitylate histone H2B via K11/K48-branched chains to maintain the open chromatin architecture necessary for the rapid transcription of self-renewal and pluripotency-associated genes following mitosis.
source: WDR5 also serves as a substrate adaptor by associating with APC/C during mitosis to ubiquitylate histone H2B via K11/K48-branched chains to maintain the open chromatin architecture necessary for the rapid transcription of self-renewal and pluripotency-associated genes following mitosis (Oh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Oh et al., 2020).

claim: In response to glutamine signaling, PASK disrupts the WDR5-APC/C interaction during mitosis, which is required for downregulating Pax7 expression and coordinating exit from self-renewal.
source: Our results suggest that, in response to glutamine signaling, PASK disrupts the WDR5-APC/C interaction during mitosis, which is required for downregulating Pax7 expression and coordinating exit from self-renewal.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing glutamine-dependent PASK nuclear translocation disrupts WDR5-APC/C and reduces Pax7 expression.

claim: The downstream target of PASK function, the WDR5-APC/C interaction, is a conserved feature among both mESCs and MuSCs.
source: Our parallel results in ES cells further suggest the generalizability of PASK function to stem cells of varied tissue origins since the downstream target of PASK function, the WDR5-APC/C interaction, is a conserved feature among both mESCs and MuSCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on data showing similar PASK functions in both ESCs and MuSCs.

claim: Transient inhibition of PASK in both mESCs and MuSCs increases the differentiation-capable progenitor population.
source: Transient inhibition of PASK in both mESCs and MuSCs increases the differentiation-capable progenitor population, providing a potential rationale for PASKi to be used for future therapeutic applications for the maintenance of stem cell function.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased stemness and enhanced differentiation potential after PASKi withdrawal in ESCs (Figure 1A-B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and MuSCs.
